description: Er Sogotokh, 'the Lonely Man,' is the first human and ancestor-hero of Sakha (Yakut) oral epic, the olonkho. The earliest olonkho printed in the West, published by Otto von Böhtlingk in 1851, tells how the solitary first man struggles against hostile spirits and secures fire, horses and a family line for his descendants, founding the human lineage of the Sakha people.
source: doi.org/10.2753/aae1061-1959350257 (Er Sogotokh); Wikipedia 'Olonkho'
research_notes: Fully attested and correctly attributed. Er Sogotokh is the first human and ancestor of the Sakha in the olonkho epic tradition; the first olonkho printed in the West was the Er Sogotokh text published by Otto von Böhtlingk in 1851, with further recordings by Iastremskii (1895) and in 1927-65. He defeats hostile spirits and establishes human society, so the record's 'first human hero, founder of the Sakha' summary is sound.

description: Erlik Khan (Erlik) is the great god of death and the underworld, Tamag, in Turkic and Mongolian belief. Brother of the creator Ülgen, he rules the dead below the earth, sends plague and evil spirits against the living, and is propitiated by Buryat, Khakas and Mongolian shamans who seek to travel safely between the worlds of the living and the dead.
source: Wikipedia 'Erlik'; Vértes 1990 (Khakas/Buryat tradition)
research_notes: Fully attested. Erlik is the Turkic god of death and the underworld (Tamag), brother of Ülgen, creator of the first human and god of the dead. The Khakas place his copper palace on the ninth layer of the earth, and he is actively worshiped by Buryats. The record's judge archetype fits his role as underworld judge and ruler of the dead.

description: Parikhan is the peri-princess of the Tajik fairy tale 'Shahabaskhan and Parikhan.' Left abandoned in the forest by the khan's men, she is saved by the hero Shahabaskhan, and their romance unfolds in the manner of the peri tales of Persianate Central Asian storytelling, in which fairy maidens wed mortal heroes. She is a fairy princess, not a restless ghost.
source: TextGrid 'Shahabaskhan and Parikhan' (Tajik tale, Russian text)
research_notes: Attested but the record mislabels her: the input calls Parikhan a ghost of the unburied dead, but in the Tajik tale 'Shahabaskhan and Parikhan' she is a peri princess abandoned in the forest by the khan's men and rescued by the hero. She belongs to the peri (fairy) tradition of Persianate Tajik storytelling, not to ghost-lore. Attested via the digitized TextGrid text.

description: Palden Lhamo (Śrīdēvī), the 'Glorious Goddess,' is the principal female protector deity of Tibetan Buddhism and the only woman among the Eight Guardians of the Dharma. A wrathful form of Tara, she rides a mule across a sea of blood, bearing a sword and skull cup, guarding the Dalai Lamas and the lineage of the Buddhist teaching.
source: Wikipedia 'Palden Lhamo'
research_notes: Fully attested and correctly attributed to Tibetan Buddhism. Palden Lhamo is the only female among the Eight Guardians of the Dharma and the principal protectress of Tibet; she is a wrathful emanation of Tara. A famous episode tells how her mule received a wound when she slew the demon-king of Lanka, and she is the dharmapala of the Dalai Lamas.

description: Qarakorshaq is a monster of Turkic folklore said to lurk in dark hollows, abandoned houses and hidden pits, seizing and devouring anyone who draws near at night. It is driven off by light and noise. Some scholars read the creature as folk memory of large animals now extinct in Central Asia, which explains its shadowy presence in herding lore.
source: K. Bazylkhan, 'Qarakorshaq' (Turkic folklore); Turkmen oral tradition
research_notes: Attested in Turkic folklore studies. Qarakorshaq is described as a creature of dark holes and abandoned houses that seizes and devours its victims and is scared off by light and noise. Some scholars treat it as folk memory of now-extinct real animals. The record's vague 'forest monster of Turkmenistan' framing fits this attested core.

description: Dayan Deerh is a shamanic deity of fertility and protection from the Khövsgöl region of northern Mongolia, venerated in both yellow and black shamanism. Worshipped as a mountain god turned shaman-spirit and community guardian, his cult centers on Tsagaannuur and the Deerkhiin Khüree shrine, where his statue and renewed ongons receive offerings for cattle and children.
source: Wikipedia 'Dayan Deerh'; D. S. Zhambalsuren (Mongolian shamanism)
research_notes: Fully attested. Dayan Deerh is a fertility and protection deity of Khövsgöl, Mongolia, who developed from a mountain god into a shaman-spirit and later a protector of the community. He is central to both yellow and black shamanism; his statue cult is located at Tsagaannuur / Deerkhiin Khüree, where the ongons are renewed every three years. The record's summary is accurate.

description: Hızır (Khidr), the 'Green One,' is the mysterious immortal guide of Turkic and Islamic tradition, revered across Turkmen lands as the patron of travelers and the helper who appears when he is truly needed. On Hıdırellez, the sixth of May, he is honored as the renewer of spring and the bringer of good fortune.
source: khidr.org 'Hizir'; Turkmen oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Hızır (Khidr) is a central figure of Turkic and Islamic piety, described as among the most revered figures after the Prophet and Ali among Turks; he is patron of travelers and appears when genuinely needed, never when summoned. The May 6 celebration (Hıdırellez) marks him as renewer of spring and bringer of fortune.

description: The crane (turna) is a sacred and deeply revered bird of Uzbek and wider Turkic folklore, celebrated as a messenger of spring and of news from home and as a symbol of fidelity and longing. Its migration and calling fill songs of separation and hope; the title of a named guardian spirit is a modern addition to this older bird cult.
source: Şükrü Elçin, 'Türk Halk Edebiyatında Turna Motifi' (turuz.com)
research_notes: The turna crane is attested as a sacred bird in Turkic folk literature (Elçin, 'Turna Motifi'): primarily a messenger motif and a symbol of gurbet, longing for home, with roots in the totemist and shamanic era, plus crane personal names and toponyms across Anatolia and Central Asia. No named 'guardian' crane spirit appears in Uzbek sources; that title is a modern addition to genuine crane reverence. Marked attested on the strength of the real bird cult.

description: In Kazakh tradition the crane (turna) is an honored bird of the steppe, its cry read as a voice of longing and its spring arrival as a promise of renewal. The picture of a crane spirit watching over lakes and rivers grows from this reverence and from Turkic belief in bird spirits that tend the waters, though no such named guardian is recorded in Kazakh sources.
source: Şükrü Elçin, 'Türk Halk Edebiyatında Turna Motifi'; Kazakh oral tradition
research_notes: The turna crane is an honored bird across Kazakh and Turkic tradition, appearing as messenger of spring and voice of longing in songs and epics (Elçin). No named 'crane water-spirit' appears in Kazakh sources; the entry grafts a water-spirit archetype onto real crane reverence. Marked attested for the underlying bird cult, with the water-spirit framing corrected in the description.

description: The celestial deer of Mongolia is the leaping, antlered stag carved on the Bronze Age deer stones that stand across the northern steppe, monuments some three thousand years old. Scholars such as William Fitzhugh interpret these 'flying deer' as spirit beings that carry the souls of warriors and leaders toward the heavens, making the deer a creature of the upper world.
source: Wikipedia 'Deer stones'; W. Fitzhugh, Smithsonian deer-stone research
research_notes: Attested through archaeology and scholarship. The Bronze Age deer stones of Mongolia (c. 3000 years old) bear leaping stag carvings; Fitzhugh and the Smithsonian interpret them as 'spirit deer' that carry warrior souls skyward, linking the carvings to celestial and afterlife symbolism. The record's 'soul-carrying spirit deer' fairly summarizes that interpretation.

description: Chura-Batyr is the epic hero of the Tatar people, rooted in the historical figure Chura Narykov of the sixteenth-century Kazan Khanate. Tales present him as a defender of the Tatar lands, a warrior of great strength and loyalty whose downfall through betrayal became a byword for resistance and lament in Tatar oral tradition.
source: Wikipedia 'Chura-Batyr'; Tatar oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Chura-Batyr is a Tatar epic hero rooted in the historical Chura Narykov of the sixteenth-century Kazan Khanate, with legends associating him with the defense of Kazan. The 'against Ivan the Terrible' framing is a popular simplification, since the historical Chura predates the 1552 fall of Kazan; the epic treats him as a loyal warrior undone by betrayal.

description: Chyskhaan is the Lord of Cold in Sakha (Yakut) belief, a spirit who rules the fierce frosts of Siberia and dwells in an ice palace said to stand near Oymyakon, one of the coldest inhabited places on earth. When his breath thickens and his horns gather frost, the deepest cold of winter is said to be drawing near.
source: Wikipedia 'Chyskhaan'; Sakha winter folklore
research_notes: Attested. Chyskhaan is the Yakut Lord of Cold whose ice palace near Oymyakon, one of the coldest inhabited places, is a genuine element of Sakha winter folklore; frost on his horns is read as a sign of approaching extreme cold. The modern Father Frost makeover is secondary to the older spirit of frost.

description: The celestial moose is the great elk of Evenki star-lore, read in the constellation of the Big Dipper. In the best-known telling the heavenly hunter Mangi pursues the elk across the sky, the Milky Way is his ski track, and the turning of the northern heavens retells their endless chase, a story of the hunt that shaped the world above.
source: Y. Berezkin, star-lore motif database; Evenki oral tradition (Mangi)
research_notes: Attested. Evenki star-lore (Berezkin's motif database) makes the Big Dipper an elk or moose pursued by the hunter Mangi, with the Milky Way as his ski track and the chase explaining the turning of the northern sky. The record's 'moose carries the sun' detail is a conflation; the core celestial-elk tradition is genuine.

description: Among the Nenets of Siberia the bright northern stars are read as a celestial reindeer or elk pursued across the sky, a tale told by forest Nenets reindeer herders to mark the turning of the seasons. Because the reindeer stands at the heart of Nenets life, its image in the heavens carries both practical and sacred meaning.
source: Y. Berezkin, star-lore motif database (forest Nenets); Nenets oral tradition
research_notes: Attested with caution. Star-lore reading the northern constellations as a hunted elk or reindeer is documented among forest Nenets and neighboring reindeer-herding peoples (Berezkin), while tundra Nenets are recorded as unfamiliar with an animal reading of the stars. The 'seven reindeer' framing is a simplification; the reindeer's central place in Nenets cosmology supports a celestial-reindeer reading.

description: Not independently attested as a deity of Uzbek folklore. No source records an owl god in Uzbek tradition, and owls are generally birds of ill omen in Central Asian folk belief. The closest real practice is the protective use of owl feathers against the evil eye, a charm best documented among the neighboring Kazakh people rather than in any Uzbek owl cult.
source: None — no independent source; cf. Kazakh owl-feather beliefs (dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/ayt/article/1627544)
research_notes: No source records an owl deity in Uzbek folklore; the record is template-generated, with empty appearance and behavior and a contradictory water-spirit archetype. Owls are generally ill-omened birds in Central Asian belief. The real protective owl-feather charm against the evil eye is documented among the Kazakhs (dergipark article on Kazakh owl beliefs). Marked unattested.

description: Not independently attested as a giant in Kazakh folklore. Kazakh tradition instead holds the owl (üki) sacred: owl feathers are fastened to cradles and headdresses to shield newborns, children and young brides from evil spirits, and to guard akyns, the poet-singers, from harm. No giant owl figure appears in recorded Kazakh tales.
source: None — no independent source; cf. Kazakh üki beliefs (dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/ayt/article/1627544)
research_notes: No owl giant appears in Kazakh sources; the record is template filler. The genuine Kazakh owl tradition is the sacred üki: owl feathers protect children, brides and akyns from evil spirits and the evil eye, and related idioms remain in daily use. Marked unattested; the üki tradition is the correct analogue.

description: The ongon, plural ongod, is the spirit of Mongolian and Siberian shamanism housed in a consecrated idol and tended like a living being. Deceased shamans become ongod, and black shamans summon their spirits up while drumming in trance. Ongod are felt to dwell in liminal places, at river mouths and on the borders between taiga and steppe.
source: Wikipedia 'Ongon'
research_notes: Attested. The ongon (plural ongod) is a central Mongolian shamanic spirit housed in a consecrated idol; deceased shamans become ongod. Black shamans call ongod up while drumming in trance, yellow shamans also revere them, and the spirits are felt to dwell in liminal places such as river mouths and taiga-steppe borders. The record's spirit-helper framing is accurate.

description: Not independently attested as a scorpion spirit in Tajik folklore. The word zambur (zambūr) simply means 'wasp' in Persian, and no Tajik tale records a desert scorpion spirit by this name. Real scorpion lore in the region is confined to folk warnings about the black scorpion's sting and its place in proverbs and sayings.
source: None — no independent source; 'zambur' = wasp (Persian)
research_notes: No Tajik scorpion spirit named 'Zambur' was found in any source; zambur (zambūr) is the Persian word for wasp, and the record appears to be template-generated filler. The closest real material is general Islamic and Central Asian folk lore about scorpion stings. Marked unattested.

description: Zhalmauyz (Zhalmauyz Kempir) is the ogress of Kazakh folklore, an ancient cannibal hag who hunts for children to devour. She has seven heads, a single eye and hoof-like feet, and she shifts her shape to deceive her victims. Her name, echoing the steppe word for a child-stealing bogey, is used to frighten the young.
source: Wikipedia 'Zhalmauyz'; Kazakh oral tradition
research_notes: Attested and well documented, but the record's 'spirit of the camel, protector of herds' is wrong. Zhalmauyz (Zhalmauyz Kempir) is the Kazakh ogress: seven heads, one eye, hooves, cannibal, shapeshifter. Cognates include Jelmogus, Dshalmaus and Jel Maja across the Turkic languages. The description corrects the misidentification.

description: The Forty Maidens (Kirk Kiz), here given the name Zuleikha, are a band of warrior women of Turkmen and neighboring Central Asian tradition who defend their stronghold against invaders. The ninth-century fortress of Kirk Kiz at Termez is linked to their tale, told across Turkmen, Karakalpak and Uzbek epic lore and praised for the maidens' courage.
source: meros.uz 'Qirq Qiz Qal'asi'; voicesoncentralasia.org 'Kirk Kiz'; Turkmen/Karakalpak epic tradition
research_notes: The Forty Maidens (Kirk Kiz) legend is attested across Turkmen, Karakalpak and Uzbek tradition; the ninth-to-tenth-century Kirk Kiz fortress at Termez is linked to it, with a princess leading forty warrior girls (meros.uz; voicesoncentralasia.org). The name 'Zuleikha' is not used in the attested versions, whose leaders are Gulaim or Gulsum; 'Zuleikha' properly belongs to the Quranic wife of Potiphar in the Yusuf-Zuleikha romance. Marked attested for the underlying legend, with the name flagged as a conflation.

description: Nyurgun Bootur, 'the Swift,' is the foremost hero of the Sakha (Yakut) epic cycle, the olonkho. A champion of the Middle World, he battles the hostile abaahy demons to defend his people and restore balance to the cosmos, aided by his swift steed and weapons forged by heavenly smiths. His songs were set down in written form by Platon Oyunsky.
source: P. Oyunsky, 'Nyurgun Bootur the Swift' (1932); Pukhov 1962; Ergis 1974
research_notes: Attested. Nyurgun Bootur the Swift is the aiyy champion of the Middle World who fights the abaahy in the olonkho; Platon Oyunsky composed the famous cantos (1932), with scholarly studies by Pukhov (1962) and Ergis (1974). The record's summary of his role as defender of the Sakha people is accurate.

description: Num is the supreme sky god of the Nenets people of Siberia, the good creator of the earth and all living things and the high god of the Nenets pantheon. In Nenets dualistic cosmology he is one of two demiurges whose malevolent son Nga rules the dead below; in one myth a shaman went to Nga's realm, wed his daughter, and became the Old Man of the Earth who upholds the world.
source: Wikipedia 'Num (god)'; Vértes 1990
research_notes: Attested. Num is the Nenets sky god and good creator, one of the two demiurges of Nenets belief; his malevolent son Nga rules the dead below the earth. In the world-sustaining myth the shaman journeys to Nga's realm, marries Nga's daughter and becomes the Old Man of the Earth; Num and Nga also create the world together in a dualistic cosmology (Wikipedia; Vértes 1990).

description: Nga is the Nenets god of death, the malevolent son of the sky god Num and one of the two demiurges of Nenets belief. His domain lies below the earth, where the dead go. In a celebrated myth a shaman journeys to Nga's realm, marries Nga's daughter and becomes the Old Man of the Earth, while Num and Nga together shape the world in a tale of dualistic cosmology.
source: Wikipedia 'Nga (god)'; Vértes 1990
research_notes: Attested. Nga is the Nenets god of death, the malevolent son of Num and the second demiurge; his domain is below the earth. The shaman's journey to Nga's realm to marry his daughter is the pivot of the world-supporting myth (Wikipedia 'Nga (god)'; Vértes 1990). The record's 'spreads disease, steals souls' summary overstates details not found in the sources, but the underworld-god role is sound.

description: Nyenchen Thanglha is the great mountain god of Tibet, lord of the Nyenchen Thanglha range and chief of the nyen spirits. A white-clad warrior who rides a white horse, he was a wrathful native deity before he bound himself by oath before Padmasambhava and became a protector of the Buddhist teaching, called upon for protection, good fortune and fair weather.
source: Wikipedia 'Nyenchen Thanglha'; Academia.edu 'Thang lha' (Nyingma Byang gter)
research_notes: Attested. Nyenchen Thanglha is the chief nyen mountain god of Tibet, bound by oath before Padmasambhava to protect the Dharma; his roles progress from srung ma (protector) to sku lha (personal god) to gter bdag (treasure-lord), with the secret name rDo rje 'bar ba rtsal (Academia.edu Byang gter study). The white-robed warrior on a white horse is the standard depiction.

description: Not independently attested as a guardian spirit in Kazakh folklore. The felines that carry mythic weight across the Altai and Turkic world are the lynx, the manul or Pallas's cat, and the snow leopard, dark beasts said in Altai tradition to have been created by the deity of the underworld and surrounded by hunting prohibitions. No specific wildcat guardian appears in Kazakh sources.
source: None — no independent source; cf. doi.org/10.25205/2312-6337-2024-2-87-99 (Altai Felidae)
research_notes: No wildcat guardian spirit appears in Kazakh sources. The felines mythologized across the Altai and Turkic world are the manul, lynx and snow leopard, 'black (dark)' beasts said to be created by the underworld deity, with hunting prohibitions and symbolism of power (Oynotkinova, Altai Felidae study). Marked unattested.

description: Not independently attested as a nature-spirit in Uzbek folklore. Across the Altai and Turkic world the wild cats, above all the lynx and snow leopard, are mythologized as powerful and untamable beasts hedged about with respect and hunting customs, but no named wildcat nature-spirit is recorded for Uzbek tradition. The claimed water powers are unsupported.
source: None — no independent source; cf. doi.org/10.25205/2312-6337-2024-2-87-99 (Altai Felidae)
research_notes: No wildcat nature-spirit is recorded for Uzbek tradition. Real feline symbolism in the region concerns the lynx, manul and snow leopard as powerful, mythologized beasts with ritual prohibitions (Altai Felidae study). The template text, with a lake habitat and drowning and water powers, is filler. Marked unattested.

description: Not independently attested as a trickster in Kazakh folklore. The sly-animal role in Turkic Central Asian tales belongs to the fox, while the wild cats of the steppe appear as emblems of strength, power and freedom rather than as tricksters. No wildcat trickster is recorded in Kazakh sources; the claimed shapeshifting traits are unsupported.
source: None — no independent source; cf. Kazakh fox trickster tales
research_notes: No wildcat trickster is recorded in Kazakh folklore; the sly-animal role in Turkic tales belongs to the fox. Wild cats appear as emblems of strength and power, not as tricksters. The record's shapeshifter archetype and cliff-guardian traits are template filler. Marked unattested.

description: Not independently attested as a water-spirit in Uzbek folklore. Cats in Central Asian folk belief are domestic creatures whose favor or displeasure is read in omens, but no feline spirit of rivers or lakes appears in Uzbek tradition. The record's ocean habitat and storm-calling powers are modern inventions built on the wildcat's secretive character.
source: None — no independent source
research_notes: No feline water-spirit is attested in Uzbek tradition; the record is template filler, with an ocean habitat and drowning, water-breathing and storm powers. Cats in Central Asian belief are domestic omen animals, not water spirits. Marked unattested.

description: The wolf (qasqyr, böri) is the paramount sacred animal of Kazakh folklore, a totem descended from the ancient Turkic böri cult. Revered as a protector and as a sign of freedom and strength, the wolf appears throughout Kazakh tales, names and customs; its skin and body parts served as talismans and folk remedies, and the wolf endures as a symbol of the Kazakh people.
source: doi.org/10.26577/jh.2024.v113i2-018 (Kazakh wolf cult); Secret History of the Mongols
research_notes: The wolf (qasqyr/böri) is the paramount totemic animal of Kazakh tradition, with a documented ancient Turkic böri cult and continuing reverence (doi.org/10.26577/jh.2024.v113i2-018): skins tanned and hung at home, winter garments sewn from wolf fur, and wolf parts used in folk medicine. The 'nature-spirit' title is a modern framing of a totem rather than a named localized spirit, so the being is attested while the label is adjusted.

description: The Wind Horse (lungta) is the sacred steed of Tibetan tradition that carries fortune and the vitality of the living upward to the gods. Its image, a galloping horse bearing a flaming jewel, flies on the five-colored prayer flags of the Himalayas, where the fluttering of the lungta is said to scatter blessings, good fortune and merit across the land.
source: tibetpolicy.net 'A Short Note on Lungta'; Wikipedia 'Wind Horse'
research_notes: Attested. The lungta (rLung-rta, 'wind horse', originally kLung-rta 'river-horse') is the divine horse that carries fortune and vital force to the gods; it flies on five-colored prayer flags (yellow, green, red, white, blue) across Himalayan Vajrayana cultures (tibetpolicy.net). Tradition distinguishes a positive running Lungta from a negative fallen one. The record's prayer-flag framing matches the attested lore.

description: Börte Chino, the Blue-Grey Wolf, is the divine ancestor of the Mongols. According to the Secret History of the Mongols, the wolf and the doe Qo'ai Maral came together in love, crossed the sea, and settled at the head of the Onon river near the holy mountain Burkhan Khaldun, where their descendants, the Mongol people, arose.
source: Secret History of the Mongols; academia.edu/145780281 (Börte Chino)
research_notes: Attested. The Secret History of the Mongols opens with Börte Chino (the blue-grey wolf) and Qo'ai Maral (the fallow doe), who came together in love, crossed the sea and settled at the head of the Onon near Burkhan Khaldun, becoming the ancestors of the Mongols. Scholarship dates this arrival to the 780s (academia.edu study). The record's summary is accurate.

description: Burkhan Khaldun, in the Khentii mountains of northeastern Mongolia, is the holiest mountain of the Mongols, the birthplace and reputed burial place of Genghis Khan and one of four sacred peaks of the land. Spirits are said to dwell upon it, their presence marked by ovoo cairns, and pilgrims approach it with reverence after rites begun on the banks of the Kherlen river.
source: UNESCO WHC 1440 (Burkhan Khaldun); Secret History of the Mongols
research_notes: Attested. Burkhan Khaldun in Khentii, northeastern Mongolia, is a UNESCO-listed sacred mountain, the birthplace and reputed burial site of Genghis Khan and one of the four sacred mountains of Mongolia, marked with ovoo cairns; pilgrims begin their approach at a bridge over the Kherlen river (WHC 1440). The record's 'spirits of the mountain' framing matches Mongol reverence for its lords.

description: Barchin (Barchinoy, Oy Barchin) is the heroine of the Alpamysh epic, daughter of Boysar and the model of the brave and loyal woman of Turkic tradition. She wins her hero through contests of archery, wrestling and skill, resists a forced marriage, and holds the people together in his absence; her mausoleum still stands near the site of old Sighnoq.
source: inlibrary.uz 'Barchin'; wos.academiascience.org; Wikipedia 'Alpamysh'
research_notes: Attested. Barchin (Barchinoy/Oy Barchin/Barchin suluv) is the heroine of the Alpamysh epic, daughter of Boysar/Baysari; she is brave, resists forced marriage, and in some accounts ruled the Oghuz. Her mausoleum lies southeast of Sighnoq (inlibrary.uz; wos.academiascience.org). The record's summary of the ideal woman of Turkic epic is accurate.

description: Baychibar is the magic horse of Alpamysh in the Turkic epic of that name. Bought as a scrawny colt, he grows into a matchless steed who carries Alpamysh to win Barchin's contests, speaks to give counsel, and warns of treachery on the long roads of the tale; no unworthy rider can mount him, and he is Alpamysh's truest companion.
source: Wikipedia 'Alpamysh'
research_notes: Attested. Baychibar is Alpamysh's magic horse who wins the bayga race despite the rival's nails-in-hooves trick and later advises, warns and rescues his master; the Siberian variant is Gulibairsen (Wikipedia 'Alpamysh'). The record's speaking-horse summary is accurate.

description: Bakai is the wise elder and counselor of the Kyrgyz epic of Manas, the voice of reason among the heroes. In the episode of his meeting with Manas, he advises the young leader to unite the Kyrgyz clans and return to their homeland of Ala-Too, restoring the people's strength and power; his counsel shapes the destiny of the epic's hero.
source: open.kg 'The Meeting of Manas with Koshoy and Bakay'; Manas epic
research_notes: Attested. Bakai is the wise elder-counselor of the Manas epic; in the episode 'The Meeting of Manas with Koshoy and Bakay' (open.kg poetic retelling) he advises Manas to unite the Kyrgyz clans, return to the Ala-Too homeland and restore power, in the company of the elder Koshoy-khan. The record's counselor framing is accurate.
